title: Two Pointers & Sliding Window (Depth Pass)
relevance: High (contest-form variants of OA sliding-window / pair-counting; trains the “find the monotone trick” skill Striver/LC miss).
company_notes: OA reskins include counting subarrays with ≤k distinct IDs/SKUs (CSES Distinct Values II / Longest k-Good Segment), longest session with at most k bad events (replacement/zero-flip window), pairs of scores differing by at most D (sorted two pointers / Close Tuples after a transform), and deleting one contiguous bad segment to make all unique (Uniqueness keep-prefix + keep-suffix).

phases.goal: Spot depth-pass two-pointer / sliding-window forms when monotonicity is hidden behind constraints, sorts, or counting reductions.

must_hit.point: Recognize a contiguous constraint that is monotone in an endpoint, or when counting valid subarrays reduces to: for each R, find the farthest/closest valid L.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says the window/endpoint moves only one way as R grows, and counting becomes farthest/closest L per R.

must_hit.point: Recognize sorted pair/tuple or greedy-match settings where sorted values let you advance one pointer only forward (or match from ends) without resetting.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions sort then monotone L advance for inequalities, or end-to-end greedy matching after sort.

must_hit.point: Recognize “delete one segment / one edit” and forbidden-pair / foe-pair segment families as the same L/R window idea with a left-endpoint constraint.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps Uniqueness-style one-segment delete or foe-pair segments to a constrained left bound that only moves right.

probes: What in the statement tells you this is a sliding-window / two-pointer depth variant rather than a plain array scan?
When would you expect forbidden pairs or one-segment delete to still be a two-pointer problem?

hints.1: Look for a contiguous range whose validity only gets worse as you extend an end.
hints.2: Ask whether for each right endpoint there is a farthest or closest valid left, or whether sorting makes one pointer monotone.
hints.3: Say: contiguous monotone-in-endpoint constraints; sorted forward-only pointer advances; or for each R find farthest/closest valid L (including foe-pair / one-delete framings).

phases.goal: Choose the right window transform: at-most difference, conflict-prefetch, sorted counting, greedy match, or non-monotone-sum alternatives.

must_hit.point: Exactly-k often equals at_most(k) minus at_most(k−1) (distinct values, number of 1s, etc.): implement one window and call it twice.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States exactly(k) = at_most(k) − at_most(k−1) and reuses one at-most implementation.

must_hit.point: Forbidden-pair / foe-pair segments: for each R, L cannot go left of the latest conflicting index; answer adds R−L+1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefetches latest conflict / max forbidden left per R, then counts with ans += R−L+1.

must_hit.point: XOR equals SUM iff no bit collisions (carry-free); maintain OR/AND or per-bit occupancy and shrink when a bit repeats.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains carry-free XOR=SUM window and shrinks on repeated bits / occupancy.

must_hit.point: Sorted pair/tuple counts: fix R (or value), find minimal L with a[R]−a[L] ≤ Δ (two pointers or binary search), then add combinations such as C(len, k−1); Close Tuples easy uses a[R]−a[L]≤2 and C(cnt,2).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Fixes R, monotone-finds L under the difference bound, adds combination counts.

must_hit.point: Greedy kangaroo / match-points: sort, match largest residual to the largest feasible partner from the other end — correctness of the greedy choice is the non-obvious part.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes sort + both-ends matching and calls out greedy correctness, not pointer syntax.

probes: How do you reduce exactly-k distinct (or exactly-k ones) to a standard window?
For foe pairs, what do you precompute before the R sweep, and what do you add per R?

hints.1: Think about whether the hard part is transforming the condition before the pointers move.
hints.2: Separate templates: at_most difference, latest-conflict L, sorted difference + combinations, and greedy end matching.
hints.3: exactly(k)=at_most(k)−at_most(k−1); foe pairs tighten L by latest conflict and add R−L+1; XOR=SUM needs carry-free bit occupancy; sorted counts fix R and advance L under a[R]−a[L]≤Δ.

phases.goal: Implement amortized O(1) window updates, conflict prefetch, and monotone sorted advances without resetting L.

must_hit.point: Maintain frequency plus distinct count (or bit occupancy) so each L/R step is O(1) amortized.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Updates a freq map / distinct (or bit occupancy) on expand/shrink in amortized O(1).

must_hit.point: For each R, compute maximal (or minimal) valid L and, when counting subarrays, add R−L+1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes the per-R L update then ans += R−L+1 (as in at-most-k distinct count).

must_hit.point: After sorting, advance only the left pointer for pair/tuple inequalities; never reset.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sorted scan moves L only forward across increasing R.

must_hit.point: Prefetch per-index latest-conflict arrays for forbidden-pair segment counts before the main sweep.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Builds a latest-forbidden-left array, then runs the R loop against that bound.

must_hit.point: Opposite-direction string delete (Backspace): simulate from the right with parity of skips — still two pointers, not a stack rewrite.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Matches from the right using backspace skip parity with two indices.

probes: Walk through the freq/distinct updates when R advances and L shrinks for at-most-k distinct.
Why must the left pointer only move forward after sorting for pair-difference counts?

hints.1: Each pointer move should update a small amount of window state, not rescan.
hints.2: Name the state: freq + distinct (or bits), latest conflict bound, or monotone L after sort.
hints.3: Freq/distinct (or bit occupancy) for amortized O(1) steps; per R add R−L+1; sorted pair counts never reset L; foe pairs use prefetched latest conflict; Backspace matches from the right with skip parity.

phases.goal: State the amortized per-step window cost and when an upgrade beyond one two-pointer pass is needed.

must_hit.point: With freq + distinct (or bit occupancy), each L/R step is O(1) amortized.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says amortized O(1) per pointer step via constant-time state updates.

must_hit.point: Optional upgrade: after computing farthest reachable end with two pointers, binary lifting on that sparse table upgrades to min cuts / jumps.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions farthest-reach array then sparse table / binary lifting for multi-jump or min-cut queries (Cut).

probes: What is the per-step cost of a correct at-most-k distinct window if freq and distinct are maintained properly?
When do you layer binary lifting on top of a two-pointer farthest-reach array?

hints.1: Cost should follow from how much work each L or R move does.
hints.2: Amortized constant updates first; multi-jump queries are a separate upgrade on farthest reach.
hints.3: Each L/R step O(1) amortized with freq/distinct or bit occupancy; farthest-reach then sparse table / binary lifting for min cuts/jumps.

phases.goal: Avoid forcing shrink-only windows on non-monotone sums and other common depth-pass traps.

must_hit.point: Negative sums break classic shrink-on-sum; use prefix minima, binary search on length, or reset empty windows carefully (ATM and Students).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Refuses shrink-only when negatives appear; switches to prefix / BS-on-length / careful empty-window handling.

must_hit.point: When sums are non-monotone, switch to prefix sums + BS / deque — do not force a shrink-only window.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly abandons monotone shrink and names prefix + BS or deque.

must_hit.point: Greedy match: decide which end is the scarce resource before coding the pointers; correctness is non-obvious, not the pointer motion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks the scarce end / feasibility rule first (e.g. Counting Kangaroos 2·small≤large), then implements matching.

must_hit.point: XOR == SUM only with no bit collisions; shrinking must track repeated bits, not treat XOR like an ordinary sum window.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out carry-free occupancy and shrink-on-bit-repeat rather than sum thresholds.

probes: What goes wrong if you apply classic positive-sum shrink logic when array values can be negative?
Before coding kangaroo/match-points pointers, what must you decide about the two ends?

hints.1: Ask whether extending/shrinking the window is still monotone in the objective.
hints.2: Negatives and XOR carries break the usual shrink invariant; greedy matching needs the scarce-end choice first.
hints.3: Negatives → prefix minima / BS-on-length / careful reset (ATM and Students), not shrink-only; non-monotone sums → prefix + BS/deque; greedy: pick scarce end first; XOR=SUM needs carry-free bit occupancy.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer implementing one at_most window and calling it for k and k−1 to get exactly-k (distinct values, number of 1s, etc.) instead of specially coding an exactly-k window from scratch.

tradeoffs.topic: classic shrink-on-sum vs prefix / BS / deque
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use shrink-only windows only while the constraint is monotone; when negatives or non-monotone sums appear, switch to prefix minima, binary search on length, deque, or careful empty-window resets rather than forcing shrink-only.

tradeoffs.topic: two pointers alone vs two pointers + binary lifting
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Two pointers give farthest reachable ends / maximal valid segments; when you need min cuts or multi-jump queries, build a farthest-reach array and upgrade with a sparse table / binary lifting.

tradeoffs.topic: stack rewrite vs reverse two pointers for Backspace
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Backspace-style delete can stay two pointers: simulate from the right with parity of skips, rather than rewriting as an explicit stack rebuild.

tradeoffs.topic: pointer mechanics vs greedy correctness in matching
tradeoffs.strong_answer: In kangaroo / match-points problems, the hard part is justifying which end is scarce and that the greedy pairing is correct; the two-pointer motion is secondary.

gotchas.trap: Applying classic shrink-when-sum-too-large logic when values can be negative.
gotchas.correction: Negatives break monotone shrink; use prefix minima, binary search on length, or carefully reset empty windows (ATM and Students).

gotchas.trap: Forcing a shrink-only sliding window whenever the problem mentions subarray sums.
gotchas.correction: If sums are non-monotone, switch to prefix sums + BS / deque instead of shrink-only.

gotchas.trap: After sorting for pair/tuple inequalities, resetting the left pointer for each R.
gotchas.correction: Advance only the left pointer forward; never reset.

gotchas.trap: Treating XOR==SUM windows like ordinary sum windows without tracking bit collisions.
gotchas.correction: XOR equals SUM iff carry-free; maintain OR/AND or per-bit occupancy and shrink when a bit repeats.

gotchas.trap: Rewriting Backspace matching as a stack problem by default.
gotchas.correction: Simulate from the right with parity of skips — still two pointers.

gotchas.trap: Coding greedy end-matching pointers before deciding which end is the scarce resource.
gotchas.correction: Decide the scarce end / feasibility rule first; correctness of the greedy match is the non-obvious part.

gotchas.trap: Counting forbidden-pair segments without prefetching conflict bounds.
gotchas.correction: Prefetch per-index latest-conflict (max forbidden left) so for each R, L cannot go left of that index, then add R−L+1.
